utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm sorry to keep you all waiting. There were various administrative matters which we had to discuss. One of the problems of this Tribunal is the amount of administration, which might be done by other bodies in a national jurisdiction, which has to be done by the Tribunal. Yes. We have an agenda, which I hope everybody else has, and what I propose was to go through the agenda, since we have it, and then to deal with any other matters, or deal with any other matters as we go through, unless anybody else wants to make an alternative submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the agenda is extremely helpful. If we're in open session, may it be prudent for us not to refer to witnesses by names, for fear that they may seek or obtain -- seek and obtain protective measures, but we can always avoid using the names because we can use the numbers of the rows in your agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can observe, while we're getting ready, that I shan't be here after the break if the hearing goes beyond the break, and therefore anything that needs my particular attention, as opposed to that of one of my colleagues well able to deal with anything, then it should be raised before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I hope we'll be finished well before the break. Now, the first items are those which appear at 1 to 3. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1 and 4 are the two witnesses currently to be dealt with by an argument known as the "dead and unwilling". It is possible that there will be one additional witness whose circumstances are slightly different but who will also fall to be dealt with by that same argument. We have suggested from the beginning that the argument on "dead and unwilling" is best postponed to the end or towards the end of the trial so that the Chamber may know not what other evidence is expected but what other evidence has been adduced. That remains our submission, so therefore items 1, 4, and possibly this other witness, should be had in mind -- they can't really be timetabled -- had in mind for later determination. Item 2 is a witness who seeks, really, the ear of the Court in relation to whether he should give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I must say, and I'm speaking entirely for myself, we haven't discussed that at all. And it may be others may take a different view, but speaking for myself, I'm very concerned about the idea of a witness coming before the tribunal of fact and giving evidence, in effect, even if the evidence is limited to certain matters, in the absence of the Defence and the accused, who will never know -- may never know what the witness has said, and there is also the perception of a tribunal of fact hearing a witness in the absence of one of the parties. That seems to me to be a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand your concern. There seems to me, at first sight, two ways in which such a witness might be dealt with. One is the way that Your Honour has effectively identified in expressing those concerns. The other, for a witness who will be physically responsive to requests to attend, is this: He can attend. We can seek a subpoena to be issued against him, and if that subpoena is granted, he can apply to have the subpoena set aside. Now, if he makes that application here in court, presumably initially in closed session and with all the parties present, if he's prepared to come into court with the other parties present, then he could identify, maybe in general terms, his concerns, and the matter could be taken forward from there. But although I quite understand the concerns of the Chamber about any hearing that is ex parte with a witness to fact, of course I understand that, nevertheless witnesses who -- and this is the only one who fall into this particular category -- are entitled to have their concerns dealt with in an appropriate way, it may ultimately be that there is no other body but the Trial Chamber to deal with those concerns by whatever method they decide. So what will happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, concerning point 2, if I understand you correctly, you are telling us that this is a witness, if I understand you well or, rather, what you said in English, who would like to come ex parte before the Chamber to address the Chamber regarding the conditions of his testimony, whether he should testify or not. If this is to hear a witness on the conditions of his testimony personally, that has been done elsewhere in other cases and I am not opposed to it. And I'm speaking in my personal name. If we're talking about the testimony itself, that is another matter. So there are two things that we need to distinguish between. If the witness is going to tell us his concerns regarding his testimony, that is one thing, and quite another thing if he is to testify ex parte, and in this respect I support what my colleague Judge May has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why these matters can't be put into writing and, if necessary, they can be put in an ex parte document to the Chamber, and it will then be a matter for the Chamber to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That may well be possible. He's coming back, in any event, I think, in a couple of weeks' time, and if the written form is more likely to be helpful, then I'll deal with it in that way, at least in the first instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that would seem to be the simplest way to deal with it, an ex parte document to be sent to the Chamber. The Chamber may then rule upon it. If it's necessary to disclose it, it will be, or there will be argument upon the point. If not, then the Chamber can deal with it in the normal way of ex parte motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But just to reassure the Court and, indeed, my learned friends, whatever is said ex parte will not be on the subject of his evidence but only on the subject of his concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That leaves number 3 of the questions you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 3. Yes, the request for protective measures stands. I believe it's now been filed, and he's due to attend next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I think we're on to 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All binders, I think, have now gone out, and we await a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. When were they sent out, can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The final one on the international armed conflict, last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, how are the Defence placed in regard to that? Mr. Sayers, when can you reasonably expect to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me make sure that I understand what we're talking about. As I understand it, we have received one binder for Zepce, one binder for Zenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, these, as I understand it, are purely concerned with an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the international armed conflict, there are, as I previously informed the Chamber, many, many hundreds of documents, in fact, I believe in the range of about a thousand. It takes some time to look at those. Could we perhaps ask the Trial Chamber for January the 31st to give a written response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we can put that into an order, we will. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't want to be irresponsible and promise that I can do it in that time, and actually I don't think that we can do it. We have received those documents, as the other desk said, the last bunch was received on or about 12 January, and at about 15 December last year, we received the first package. I'm still working on reviewing the first package because it's -- I really don't know what the exact number of pages is, but I can show you in size, it is this big of a pile, about 30 or 40 centimetres. We are working on it but the reality is that we received it in a very late phase of the proceedings, and I think that we are also entitled to some reasonable time to process those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long are you asking for, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I would ask for a term to at least the 15th or 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulty about that is that we are now coming towards the end of the Prosecution case, and they may have to call additional witnesses if the ruling is against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just -- I'm sorry, I'm interrupting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think I can do it, but, Your Honour, I know it's not really polite to ask now because it should be dealt with directly, but if we would -- and I never asked the Prosecution for that -- if we can get that material in an electronic form, I mean, at least the index which was forwarded with the documents, it could speed up our work, if that is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is not a problem. That can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll say the 15th of February for that information from the Defence. The next item, item 6, I see there is an order already that the Defence are to respond by the 25th of January. Once that's done, we can determine when argument, if any, should be heard. Number 7, what is the state?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The position on the tape is that the tape itself and its transcript, that is, the whole tape as opposed to the single passage that was served some considerable time ago, the whole tape and its transcript is in the process of final review so that the accurate transcript can be provided, and I imagine it's a day or days away from provision. The witnesses who deal with the circumstances in which the tape were prepared, one was served, I think, either yesterday or the day before and the other one is due for service immediately, having gone through the process. Those statements will then fall for consideration by my learned friends whether they challenge them or not. If they don't challenge them, then they can be read or the tape's production can otherwise be admitted. If they do challenge them, then those two witnesses will have to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that we can timetable this in a proper way, is there any reason why we shouldn't order that the tapes be served by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the tapes have been served already, maybe only the extract at the moment. The whole tape, yes, I'm quite -- I can't see any particular reason not to -- the one tape, as it is, the one long tape, I don't see any reason why it shouldn't be served tomorrow, and I very much hope that we will have the transcript reviewed and available for service either tomorrow or almost immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll say that the tape to be served tomorrow; transcript, Monday. Turning to the Defence, how long do you anticipate that you would require before you can respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would say five days thereafter, Your Honour. There is a legal issue, assuming that the tapes are in order. There are 13 other intercepts which have not been included which, based on what I have seen, will be included, presumptively from what I've heard. But regardless of that, you have the issue of the manner in which this evidence was seized and comes into court which will create a legal issue. We'll be prepared to argue that within five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the Defence to respond to admissibility within five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought then to be thinking in terms of resolving the issue the following week when I think we are sitting, the week of the 31st. Give us some idea, how long would you anticipate argument about something like that to be, an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Half an hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour to 45 minutes. Thank you very much. We'll make sure that's set aside for that week. Perhaps, Mr. Nice, you could add that into your calculations for the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be other matters. Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber's had our note on researches we've made following the last time this was discussed and what we've been able to find out about statements admitted in Kupreskic and in one other case. The Chamber will recall that in, I think, Kupreskic, statements were stamped by a court official as to the authenticity to the signature, it not being clear to us whether that was a standard stamp that exists in every court and that is available for use in exactly this type of process, we never having heard of it before and, indeed, it never having been raised by the Defence who are more knowledgable on this than us before. This week we have an investigator in the field seeing if this very process can be replicated for our case, I think probably with a witness whose statement may not be particularly contentious or falls outside those who may be contentious affidavit witnesses. Nevertheless, we are trying to replicate it this week and I'll know next week what success we have. Then if that process is available to us, it will fall for consideration whether this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. It will then fall for consideration whether that sort of statement could qualify as an affidavit. Even if it could, the question will arise whether the Defence are going to take points under 94 ter which, of course, sets out a particular regime for the introduction of affidavits that may well be impossible of performance in this case. But, nevertheless, we are doing what we can to see if this process is available to us in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Provided that matter is in hand and can be expedited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm reminded that point 8 -- we perhaps skipped point 8 but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought it was connected with 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's connected with 7 but it's, of course, a general point, a question of whether you can have part of the testimony of a witness, in this case a defendant in another case, admitted without the whole of the transcript going in and the general problem of whether you can put in a transcript in these circumstances without, as it were, adopting it in its totality for its truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that can conveniently be argued with the questions of admissibility of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm happy to do that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, before responding regarding this point, I should like you to give us your opinion regarding the question of the admissibility of statements, either affidavit statements or not, in the case of statements that are being used simply to corroborate testimony that has already been given in court. Because in our point of view, if there is no challenge, if something is not contested, if it is not being challenged, if we have already heard testimony and we simply need to corroborate things that have already been said without being contested, formally speaking, could not that be regulated in this way by statements? I apologise for interrupting. Of course, you can also respond on the other matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I thought you might be asking me that exact question, so the answer to the question is, we would like to see on a case-by-case basis the specifics. There are certainly individual statements/affidavits/some form which may not be in compliance with Rule 94 but which nevertheless, given the narrowness, the corroborative nature, the reason for them being merely to authenticate a document, that we would as a matter of courtesy, common sense, civility, say, even though it doesn't comply with 94 in a technical sense, we're prepared to agree. So the short answer is, yes, there are many, and I can see that. As to the more specific and more far-ranging, that would be a different situation. If I've answered that, I would like to move on to the Blaskic issue which, of course, Mr. Nice has, indeed, set out the framework. It may well be our position -- it may well be our position that we would want all of Blaskic's testimony admitted. The problem is we don't know what all of his testimony is. Some of it was given in closed session. The Prosecution, of course, has the benefit of knowing the entire length, breadth, and subjects covered by Colonel now General Blaskic in his testimony. If we could have the entire --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Stein, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I thought I was getting better, but I slip. If we could have the entire transcript at our disposal, if the Court could so ask the Blaskic Trial Chamber and if we could be supplied with that which we do not have, then we would make a judgement whether our position was that it all can come in, and then we can all have our various parts of it. Otherwise, I'm afraid we are left with the anomalous situation of the proponent of the testimony cherry-picking, taking some things he likes and other things he doesn't like that he says he wants in in various ways, shapes, and forms, either in the binders or other kinds of things. And, of course, you have the anomalous situation of the Prosecution, on the one hand, challenging General Blaskic's testimony, in whole or in part, in one proceeding and yet accepting it, in whole or in part, in another proceeding, and then ultimately you may get to the situation of the Blaskic Chamber rejecting, again in whole or in part, the testimony, and this Chamber being asked to rely, again in whole or in part, on his testimony. Those are issues that I think we need to air, but I don't think we're in a position to air them until we see the entire world of what's out there, in his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a simpler course, is it not, this: to see what the application is, to see what it is asked that we admit, and at that stage to make rulings, if we can, or to ask for further material, if need be? But to try at this stage, I think, to make rulings isn't going to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's certainly the logic of it, although I think Mr. Nice and I have the benefit of foresight that the Court does not, in that we know, in some of the dossiers, for instance, and in other communications, the kinds of things that Mr. Nice wants to have in. But Your Honour is right. I would much rather deal in the concrete than in the abstract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Unless there are any other matters on that page, going on to the second page of the agenda, the village dossiers or binders. Just looking at the position as far as the Chamber is concerned, we have had, of course, Tulica decided; Stupni Do and Vares, we have had; and Zenica and Busovaca, we certainly have. Zepce, my memory doesn't assist. I wonder if the legal officer can help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you assist us as to that? This is described as Busovaca and Zepce. It's not my recollection that they are together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I think you've had Zepce and it's been provided separately. Yes, Mr. Scott confirms that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's separate; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a separate binder and it's been provided separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Vitez, Kiseljak, Novi Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yet to be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- still to come. I must say my own recollection is not seeing Zepce, but we can look into that. That's one of the things perhaps we could check.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When is it proposed that we would have the last four or three?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give me one minute? We discussed this last night, and I'm not entirely -- my memory has let me down. I'll just find out. Ten days from today, I hope, for all of them. It is a very labour-intensive task, but I think ten days from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 31st of January, then. What we need to do, in this context, is to timetable, I think, a hearing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. The resolution of the crime base or the evidence is important to the overall time scale of the trial, and it's clear, from one response that we've received already, that there is going to be, I think, a root-and-branch objection to any witness statement. And accordingly the Chamber is indeed right to say that the matter should be timetabled, and it seems to us that it would be prudent or sensible to have them timetabled all on the same occasion, really, rather than try and deal with them piecemeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Assuming they are provided in ten days, then time for consideration would suggest that they certainly couldn't be argued until probably the beginning of the week of February the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that would seem to be sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think that should give us time to -- I hope that will give us time, in what's left of the trial, to call up such witnesses as may be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be sensible to identify a time. There are general principles here, and I don't think we need necessarily to go through every item in every binder, and I invite you to look at the Tulica decision as a guide as to what we're likely to find. And with that in mind, I hope we can deal with the matter fairly expeditiously, in an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. And where we've said we would intend to call, say, two witnesses per location, it may always be that the witnesses have already come or that the topics have already been covered, and there is always, of course, the prospect of relying on transcripts in other cases, subject to any objection. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be sensible to timetable the argument for the 14th of February and allow an hour for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Just before we move on, if we are going to, in fact Your Honour passed over item 10 on the first sheet, and the position there is that all exhibits will be provided, I think, by either this weekend or the end of next week. By the end of next week, although the vast majority have already been provided. Mr. Scott is continuing the process of review with Mr. Lopez-Terres and Ms. Somers. So they will all be provided by the end of next week, the vast majority having already been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say they've been provided, are these all new exhibits or are they old exhibits to form a new binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's probably a combination of documents that were provided in the original core bundle, documents that may have been provided in general circumstances at earlier stages, and some new documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they are to be provided by the 28th of January. Yes. Can the Defence assist us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It would be helpful to us if, using their electronic database, we know what they think is still outstanding. We've already met and discussed some things that we agree to and some that we don't. Because of the "Z" numbering system that Mr. Nice persuaded the Court to use, we're always at somewhat of a loss as to where we are; not a total loss, but it's an imperfect system until the end. So if we could have a little help from our opposition, we would appreciate it, specifically identifying that which is still at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure if Mr. Stein contacts Mr. Scott directly, such co-operation as it's possible for us to give will be given, because it's in everybody's interests that these documents are marshalled and decisions about them are made as swiftly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think I have in mind to say formally that the Defence respond within 14 days. It may be that it's possible to deal with this matter by discussion between counsel. I would hope it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fourteen days of what, Sir, today or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of the 28th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By "respond," I mean to indicate what is admitted and what isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll just ask the legal officer something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We note number 12. I don't think it's necessary to go into that again. Numbers 13 and 14, and I note that on the 26th of November it was thought there were about 20 witnesses, 30 sessions, six weeks, end of the first week of March 2000. Now, unless there is a change in that, that seems to be an acceptable programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think there may be a change, but I hope not very dramatic one. By my calculation of listed witnesses, that is, witnesses already notified, there are about 20 outstanding. There may be one or two deletions to come and there may be one or two non-attendances. And by our present timetable, which we know changes on a daily basis, but nevertheless, by our present timetable, those witnesses would, indeed, be concluded by the week of the 1st of March, coming into February the 28th. But that doesn't take account of any witnesses who may have to be called because of the need to establish, by live evidence, village binder material, and the Chamber will be alive to the fact that there are already indicated one or two additional witnesses of whom we've only recently had knowledge; for example, Mr. Beese, whose statement has been served, is a witness I wish to call, and obviously if there's going to be opposition to that, that argument ought to be dealt with sooner than later. The argument won't take very long, if there's any argument at all, and I would respectfully suggest that we deal with the Beese matter once the Court is fully constituted next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could raise that at a convenient and early time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll mark Beese for probably Tuesday, I would have thought, if we can fit it in around General Merdan, and I don't know yet if there is any objection to his evidence or on what grounds. Included within that 20 witnesses, there are, of course, witnesses of the type -- of the man who is going to produce the maps that the Chamber asked to be produced, there's the witness who can produce the video showing the overflight of the area, and there's another witness, one of the investigators, who, as the Defence have been notified, is preparing an analysis of some of the documents dealing with the Viteska Brigade, so they are not all witnesses of raw fact. Some of them fall into a different and, I hope, shorter category. I've got a note. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think since December 1998, we have been asking you how many witnesses you're going to call and when your case is going to finish. It is unusual to be in this position, to put it mildly, 11 months or so into the trial, where we still have not got a definite answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as to that and as to the time taken by evidence, I'm in the hands of others. As to the witnesses I'm calling, I've already given regular notices of the witnesses I'm calling and set up, in detail, the process through which we've gone. As to the witnesses required for the crime base in the villages, I am entirely in the hands of the response of the Defence, and I have taken every step to abbreviate that evidence. That leaves simply outstanding one or two witnesses who I may seek to add, and I've made it plain from the beginning that that is a reality in a case like this, and indeed the Chamber knows something already of the circumstances in which we come to hear late of material that may be of particular value to the chamber. So of course I can't give a closing date for the trial. No one ever can. My best calculation is that the listed witnesses will take us to the end of February, beginning of March, on the present timetable. I interject we have lost quite a lot of days one way and another, since the last time I think I was asked, through no fault of ours or anybody else's, and as to other witnesses, if they, in fact, extend the trial timetable, it won't be by very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me make it plain --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour asked me at an early stage roughly how many witnesses I forecast, I forecast about 100. Your Honour said at one stage that the 100 was not, in your own personal judgement, an unreasonable number, and I calculate or Ms. Verhaag calculates that, indeed, if things turn out in the way I forecast, it will be about 100. I should tell you that of the remaining witnesses in the list of 20, there is certainly the prospect, if not probability, of one or more of them being deleted either by reasons of my judgement or their non-availability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you're right about that. You also at one stage, Mr. Nice, I recollect, said that it would take a year. We expect it to take less. The 10th of March is the date that we expect you to finish your case, and speaking for the two of us, we would make an order to that effect. But we are only constituted for two, so at the moment we can't make an order. But would you have in mind that date and work towards it, that's the first week of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: You are not obliged, Mr. Nice, to go until the 10th. You can finish even before if you want. We will not oblige you to go up to the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that, and I'm sure Your Honour would understand that if it was down to me, I would have finished this Prosecution case, for matters of personal choice, a long time ago. But the Chamber must have in mind, if I may just cautiously but respectfully remind it, that we had a witness this week, examination-in-chief, less than one hour. I cannot predict and I cannot control how long the evidence takes because the Chamber will remember how long the cross-examination was, and I've done everything I can to abbreviate this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think there's one other matter about the calendar, and that is that we said that the Chamber would not be sitting in the week of the 13th to the 17th. Should it be necessary for any chance to hear any evidence or argument or anything of the sort in that week, we shall change the sitting pattern and sit that week. I hope that is an added incentive to finish on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to deal with it as an added incentive. I'm away that week; I've made private arrangements; I'm not going to be here. I very respectfully must press on the Chamber that although the desire, the understandable desire to bring this case to a conclusion is in everyone's minds, since we are only presenting evidence to assist the Chamber and to present this case and are doing so conscientiously and responsibly, we would very respectfully urge you not to bring about artificial cut-off dates -- not artificial, in any sense arbitrary cut-off dates or to impose on us pressures that are not appropriate. I will not be here that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard the point that I made. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May I inquire, sir, you mentioned the week of the 14th as a week in which we're not sitting. Perhaps my calendar is not correct. I thought we were not sitting the week of the 7th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, the week of the 7th of February. We're in March now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sorry. Just so I won't surprise my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, we do not have anything relative to the Viteska Brigade that I'm aware of, and as to Mr. Beese, I gather the issue is set down for the argument on his testimony, we do object, not his actual presentation. I want to make clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What's the objection as far as Beese is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Beese is a late witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right. Moreover, quite frankly, Judge, he's cumulative, in our view, to the presentation of the case, but that's our view of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look at that in due course. I shall write down against number 14, the 10th of March or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I wish to react to what you just said. The Chamber is not trying to stop you in an artificial or arbitrary manner, as you said, to prevent the Office of the Prosecutor in completing and conducting its work. I do not think that, quite the converse. It is our responsibility that the case is presented in as complete a manner as possible and without delay. This is one of the concerns of justice in general, not only here but wherever justice is dispensed. It should be expeditious and fair. It is within that context that we have to talk about this delay. You've already changed from February to March and you know what the consequences are. You know that quite a number of things can be corroborated by documents when this is not contested, so it is up to you to organise yourself or to organise your work. As far as we are concerned, we are not taking that recess which was envisaged so as to allow the Prosecution to finish the presentation of its case. So we shall not be taking the recess that was envisaged. That is how we see this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to reply to that. We have not delayed matters. Matters have been delayed by matters outside our control, including the loss of days at this Chamber through no fault of anyone's. Frankly, I'm disappointed that the Chamber is obliging the Prosecution to face the possibility of presenting evidence in my absence. I made it quite clear when we considered time by way of non-sitting dates that it was important for us to be able to plan our private, including our family lives. I am the senior trial attorney prosecuting this case, I have made private arrangements, and I'm frankly disappointed that in light of everything that's happened, that step's been taken. We will respond to it by making counsel available to lead evidence, but my position remains as it is. We are not responsible for the delay, delay has occurred for other reasons, and this office and this team will not accept criticism for none is properly visited upon it. That's all I'm going to say on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The matter can be resolved by finishing the Prosecution case on the 10th of March. That means 11 months will have been spent upon it, a proper time given the length of cross-examination, but I doubt if any longer would be proper. I think what it requires, if I may say so, and this is the last thing to say on the matter, is a robust decision to close the case and to rely on the very extensive evidence which you've already called. We could debate this further but we're not going to. Let's move on to the Defence. In this connection, number 15, where are we on the core documents, Mr. Sayers, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the objections that we filed on July the 6th, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber will note that the Kordic Defence and, I think, the Cerkez Defence had not stood on ceremony, we've not insisted upon technical objections to the admissibility of documents, other than in the very few instances where we've made objections to specific -- specifically to authenticity. I might draw the Trial Chamber's attention, for example, to the pleading we filed on July the 6th, Exhibit tab numbers 55, 59, 76, 89, 108, and 140. Those, frankly, Your Honour, are the only documents I think that we've objected to on authenticity grounds, and I think that given the nature of those documents, it will be self-evident why some foundation, some authentication will be required. But other than that, I do not believe that we have objected to the introduction of any of the numerous documents offered by the Prosecution, and I anticipate that that is the course that we will follow when we review the remaining documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you, within the next month, and together with the Prosecution, agree on a core bundle? This really shouldn't be something for the Trial Chamber. Then equally, if you want to add to it when it comes to your case or you want to put documents in, of course you can do so. The important thing is to have out of the 3.000-plus documents that we have, something of that order, 2.000-plus certainly, and many of them extending to many pages, the pages, and I suspect there won't be many, hundreds at the most, which are actually of significance and importance on which the parties rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The dossier, I think, we've dealt with. The evidence of Mr. Cigar, we should tabulate a date or timetable a date for argument. Again, sooner rather than later. I don't think anything has been said about this so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We were going to propose that the Cigar argument might be dealt with next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But we've already got one application, that's the Beese application, and I don't know how long the Cigar argument will take. A skeleton will be available by the beginning of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Beese argument will be, I guess, short. I can't believe it can occupy much more than a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Call it quarter of an hour. The Cigar argument, I suppose, is slightly more substantial. Half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would ask for 45 minutes. It is a substantial argument raising interesting issues. I would just ask that we have the Prosecution's skeleton argument a day or two before the scheduled hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot -- it's not normal that we should devote more time to discuss the admissibility of an expert opinion than for the expert opinion itself, that becomes rather absurd. I cannot accept that. I have read the document, I have seen your highly sophisticated manner, using various colours to comment and analyse it, we have read that. So you can tell us very briefly, in ten minutes, what the point is because we've read it all. We don't need 45 minutes to remind us what an expert opinion is. After all, we are professionals. We know what experts are, we know what kind of sources experts use, and we know all these things, what are the reliable and non-reliable sources on which one can rely and those that are not acceptable, we know all these things. So please do not explain all those things to us. After all, we're not going to spend an hour and a half to hear whether we should accept an expert opinion or not because that very expert opinion might take that much time, so personally I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The only reason I asked for 45 minutes is two-fold: First, if I ask for 45 and do it in a half hour, you will be much happier with my presentation and my speed or lack thereafter. Second, frankly, the issue of experts is, with respect to all concerned, the most perplexing issue in modern procedure. It has plagued the U.S. Supreme Court in several ways, times, shapes. It has got the benefit of our best and worst judicial thinking, and it's important, and a very important issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why we shouldn't deal with both the Beese argument and this argument on, say, next Friday, three-quarters of an hour for the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. The only reason for having it possibly earlier than that on Thursday is that if Beese is coming, we can secure his attendance more conveniently, say, for the following week by knowing about it on the Friday. But to some degree, timetableing may be affected by the way the particular witnesses are cross-examined and how much time is taken, but I'm in the Court's hands. Thursday or Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can -- I think Friday. Next Friday. Perhaps I could ask the legal officer about the next item. Yes. Judge Bennouna makes a point that if we have a break anyway, we can advance the time for that argument during the week if there becomes a better time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. Number 18. [Trial Chamber confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told that the note is a correct one against 18, that it's a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine, unless anybody wants to say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I ask that it be added only because as we approach our case, it becomes more important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it becomes more urgent. Thank you. I'll note that. Number 19, it's a matter really for the Prosecution and to draw the Prosecution's attention to Judge Hunt's decision in Krnojelac dated the 1st of November, where the Judge required the Prosecution to file a signed report by a member of the team certifying that the obligations under Rule 68 had been carried out. Is there any objection to that being done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We regard that as an entirely inappropriate procedure and one that should never have got started in these courts. I'm not going to try and sign up to a document of that kind and I don't think any of our team will. Indeed, the whole idea, which started off with an affidavit in Holland, thus incorporating the jurisprudence of another country into the jurisprudence of this Chamber, seemed to me misconceived. The position about exculpatory material is, as I've said from the beginning, difficult in this setting for the reason that the quantity of material that exists is, of course, beyond the ability of an individual or of a team to read and consider. It's far too much, and it grows every day. Further, the question of what is and what is not exculpatory is very much a matter of judgement, difficult judgement, made the more difficult, of course, when the issues are as multi-serious as they are here, and made difficult when, as here, the Defence set out, I think, a list of 28 or 38 questions that they said ought to be asked effectively of each and every document. The best that one can do is one's best to honour the obligations, and as I've made plain from the beginning, that is what we have done, are doing, and will continue to do. But there's no certification, there's no document that's going to assist that exercise, and what would such a document -- what purpose would such a document serve? None. My word will be good enough, I trust, on this topic, and if it isn't, I shall like to know why. We have done our best. We are doing our best. We will continue to do our best to honour the obligations under the Rules to make available what we judge to be exculpatory material, and that's as far as we can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may, I should like to say a few words because I really do think this is a sensitive issue. I apologise for speaking in Croatian, so it will take a little longer, but I will be brief. We have discussed this issue at some length. We have exchanged quite a quantity of correspondence with the Prosecution. I have written to them and we have talked about it, and the position is the one you have just heard. However, without entering into any details, I must say two things. First, if the Prosecution did not know at the beginning of the case but by now it certainly knows what the gist of the Cerkez defence is, I'm sure they are fully conscious of that, and if they do understand that, then they know which documents they need to search for actively, not to just sit and wait and if they come across a document from another case, or an investigator, or an agency, or as a result of these various searches that have been done all over Bosnia, and then to say, "This might be a handy document for Cerkez and let's give it to him," that is not sufficient. I must say, even regarding those documents, we haven't received any, except for a very few exceptions. I do not wish to fatigue anyone. I wouldn't enter into any legal discussions. I think the Rules are quite clear, and the practice in court has taken a certain direction. A case has been mentioned where a certain standard has been set, and I would simply like to add, by way of an example, when the Prosecution claims there's no exculpatory material and then the next day such a document is put on the table. Let me use an example; two documents that were recently produced through a witness. I'm not quite sure whether it was in open session or not, but, in any event, an intelligence officer in Stari Vitez. I won't enter into the substance of the case, but I will say this: You will remember that document. At the request of a higher command, he writes a report who, in his opinion, are war criminals or, rather, people responsible for various crimes in Vitez, and he is sitting 500 metres from the office of my client. And among the 30 names, he doesn't mention my client. When the Prosecutor and I started discussing that document, the Prosecutor says to me, "That is not exculpatory evidence. Every list that doesn't mention your client is not exculpatory." Yes, I agree with that, that every list that doesn't mention my client is not exculpatory material. But if we take into account the circumstances, who it was in question, at what time, and what the aim of such a list was, then this is a perfect example of an exculpatory document. After that, I'm afraid I cannot trust and I cannot accept that the Prosecution has, in good faith, engaged in an active search, because it all boils down to whether the Prosecution may come across a certain document or not and then it will provide it to the Defence. If it doesn't, that's the end of it. In an earlier stage of disclosure, I'm afraid last night I was too tired to find the document in question, but we received a document, and in the accompanying letter it wasn't clearly stated whether it was exculpatory or not. But there was a wording saying that it might be, and this was a document of some 15 paragraphs, compiled obviously in the Prosecution, and these paragraphs were excerpts from various reports. Somebody somewhere said such and such a thing. There is a report that such and such a thing happened. So these are just quotations from various reports without the source being indicated, who said this, when and where. Absolutely useless material. I responded at the time and said, "I'm sorry, this is not helpful to anyone." So I think this has become really crucial now, because we have seen, in the course of the proceedings, that there are documents that are exculpatory for my client and that mitigate his guilt, and I ask the Court to rule on this matter bearing in mind the fact, in particular, that the Prosecution, as a unified organisation, has control over documents which, due to various procedural reasons, have been used in other cases linked to the Lasva Valley but are under seal and to which I don't have access. So I think I have every right to assume that in the Blaskic, Kupreskic, Aleksovski cases, there are documents which I have heard referred to in the course of my investigations but which I cannot gain access to. But the Office of the Prosecutor, using your order of the 16th of February, can gain access to, but not just sitting around and waiting for a document to be placed on their table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask for the documents which you want, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had a precise list and if I were able to identify document number so and so, dated such and such, I would. But much of the information I have is along the lines of somebody saying, "During the investigation, I saw a document, an order," for instance, by General Blaskic from such and such a date, "and when I was interviewed in court, the document was produced, but that document is confidential. I was told it was confidential, and I can't talk about it," so I can't go on questioning that witness about it. I don't know where the limit is. Never in my life have I worked with this kind of attitude towards documents, "These are confidential, these are not." Sometimes you're not sure what kind of document you're dealing with if you don't have it in your hands, whether it is protected by the Court or not. If I know of a particular document, I will ask for it. But I think that there is no doubt that it is the obligation, unqualified obligation, of the Prosecution to actively search, especially now, when it is aware of the concept of our defence. I may agree that earlier on -- I think we can all agree that that is the bad side of this attitude regarding exculpatory material, the Prosecution need not know what it is. But by now, knowing what our defence will be, they know what is exculpatory material for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, in my view this is a matter with regard to which we have to presume the good faith of the Prosecution. There's no other way of approaching it. The Office of the Prosecutor is a team. It has the Chief Prosecutor at the head of it, and she organises the work within that office. Personally, I don't quite agree in identifying anyone within that team as being responsible personally, but I think that we must reckon with the good faith of the team, and the obligation is to provide all exculpatory material in their possession. If, on your side, however, you have a request regarding a document that you feel could be exculpatory and that may be in the possession of the Prosecution, you should ask for it. But that's it, that's the end of it, except if we were to give access to you to the documents, which it is not possible to do. That is how things have to function. There is no other way. For example, the production of documents that you requested from the ECMM, those documents in the possession of the Prosecutor, which were not disclosed here and which were not given to you, should be given to you directly without having to ask for them, because you did address the organisation in question for them, and if the Office of the Prosecutor has them, then they should give them to you. The only way to proceed is in a pragmatic manner. There is no other generalised rule. But I think that the good faith, let me say once again, of the Office of the Prosecutor has to be presumed as given, and we must work on the basis of that principle, that the Prosecution is working in good faith, as, of course, is the Defence in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if this comment is addressed to me, I wouldn't otherwise go on with this discussion. Of course, I believe in this bona fide approach, but one must make a distinction. Whether the Prosecution comes across a particular document in the course of its work is one thing, or should it explicitly assume the obligation. And I think an interpretation of the Rules does mean that, that somebody should be designated to work on it, even if it is at the end of the case, to look for documents under certain issues and under certain topics, and after that, to give a certificate and say, "We have carried out such and such searches." One's word is one's word, but a statement saying, "We have actively searched." Of course, the criteria are based on their good faith. "If we find something, we will disclose it." I now have no guarantees. To the contrary, if I understood my learned friend, he is saying, "We cannot search specifically for the Cerkez Defence." They can and should, because it is required of them by the Rules. That is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us try and bring this matter to a conclusion. I must say I agree with the Judge. It seems to me that if counsel, in court and robed, gives an assurance, then it is something which I, for one, am very likely to accept. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I would agree, and I want to make clear, because I want to join with Mr. Kovacic, the Prosecutor's word or good faith is not at issue. What is at issue is how does an institution, composed of many sections, some of which speak to each other, some of which don't, all of which have huge, vast quantities and arrays of information available to it, meet its affirmative obligation to search within that institution for a certain category of information, materially favourable or exculpatory evidence? It's no different than suing a corporation which has hundreds of thousands of employees and offices, and you ask, in a discovery request, for certain kinds of documents, and it is done akin to what has been suggested by the Prosecution in another setting, having a corporate officer arrive and affirm that, "This is the search I undertook in response to the discovery request to get the documents that you are entitled to in this particular civil lawsuit." As I understand it, the Prosecution has made a public request for at least one State to do just that. "What have you affirmatively done with response to orders of the Court?" Now, the parallel is clear and the difficulty is clear, particularly in the age of electronics and the electronic storage of data, and it is only made more difficult for those of us who are going to litigate into the 21st Century. But it doesn't stop by the Prosecutor saying, "There's just too much out there and we can't do it and there's a minefield out there, because we don't know what to look for, we don't know where to look for, we don't know what's exculpatory." I don't think that should be acceptable. They understand from our pleadings, our positions, what is favourable and what is not, and as honourable men and women, when they see it, they turn it over. The question is when they see it. And, as I think what Judge Hunt envisioned and what we propose, informally or formally, is an affirmative obligation followed by an affirmative act and an affirmative pleading that the work has been done. It will be impossible, I predict, to ever determine whether or not, in the bowels of all the information in the Prosecution's hands, is exculpatory material from us, and if some document at a later time turns up, or thing, the issue will turn up -- the issue will resolve, "Is it exculpatory, is it materially favourable, and would it have made a difference?" Well, we'll never know, and we don't want to be there, and we don't want to be in post-trial litigation on topics along these lines. And so I suggest again that as difficult as it is, someone must take the bull by the horns and pursue the suggestions, and now the law as encompassed in Judge Hunt's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard our reaction to it. We're not sitting as a fully-constituted Chamber and therefore we can't make an order, but that's our reaction. Can we move to 20. Already there are problems about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There are no specific outstanding problems of which I'm aware, Your Honour, other than the general issue which we would like to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention, and that is access to materials in the Lasva Valley cases which are available to the Prosecution but not available to the Defence, if, for no other reason, they would be of interest to Mr. Kordic's Defence, speaking for myself anyway, to investigate other sources of information that are available of a useful nature to the Defence. Certainly in terms of General Blaskic's evidence, that would be one example, and any other closed session testimony of a witness whose testimony the Prosecution proposes to introduce in part. It's simply impossible for us to evaluate the position intelligently unless we are able to see all of the testimony of that witness, because there may be portions of closed session testimony that we would choose to designate as well. So that's the position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look into that. I hadn't appreciated that there are some outstanding matters or may be. If there are, we'll consider them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, explain to me very precisely this matter because I'm afraid I don't quite understand. Up to now we have functioned as follows: When you have needed other evidence which may have been produced in other cases concerning the Lasva Valley, you requested them in writing frequently and we addressed the appropriate Chamber which generally replied favourably and provided the information requested. So it is up to you, within your strategy of defence, to say. You cannot tell the Chamber in general terms, "We need all the evidence" without being more specific. It is up to you on a case-by-case basis to tell us, "We need testimony, for instance, the Blaskic testimony for such and such a reason," and I think you must be specific with your request and that this should go through the normal channels, which means that this Chamber would address the other Chamber and see if there were any protective measures, that we have to impose them now. So it seems that that is how we have been functioning up to now and how you should organise yourself in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Judge, I think we are saying precisely the same thing. The question was, are there any specific matters outstanding in connection with a motion for access to the Lasva Valley materials. I'm not aware of any specific matters, and I merely raise the issue of, for example, General Blaskic's testimony as one instance where, should a request be made for introduction of particular parts of his testimony, then we would respectfully request access to all of his testimony so that we could make an evaluation of the request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The remaining items, we have a few minutes left before the break, are 21 and 22. Dealing first with 21, I think we said earlier that the pre-Defence conference should take place about a month before the end of the Prosecution case, working on the 10th of March for that. I would have in mind a date such as Friday, the 18th of February for a pre-Defence conference. That, I think, would be, what, about a month away? There should be time to prepare. Also, it would be about a month before the end of the Prosecution. I don't know how that would fit in with other people's programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously, that would fit in with our programme. All I'd ask is that because of the constraints of time on us for evidence, that if it's necessary to use the afternoon of the Friday, I know that that was once ventilated as a possibility on the sitting times, it's fair to, say, use the afternoon for the pre-trial conference because evidence would consume the morning, that that be considered, because otherwise we lose, of course, another chunk of time for our witnesses. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, personally, I must leave before the 18th. If I'm unavailable, someone else, obviously, from our team will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you. Would you prefer that it be dealt with earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: A day or so would certainly be helpful. I'm entirely within the Court's hands. I don't want my personal situation to affect anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter which need take a great deal of time, more than half an hour or so, I would hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: A preliminary conference, I would presume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A preliminary conference could occupy about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, one way of dealing with this, Judge Bennouna suggests and I agree, would be to deal with the matter earlier in the week, one day after our normal sitting times. If we had a break at 4, we could come back at 4.15 on, say, Wednesday the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a preliminary half-hour conference, that would be perfectly appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. So we will fix that, the 16th, Wednesday, the 16th, at 4.15. It will be subject to discussion with the interpreters, of course, who may have a view about the whole matter. But subject to satisfactory arrangements being made, that's what we would have in mind on the basis that the hearing would last about half an hour or so. Can I go on to the last item and mention in this connection that one of the matters which this Trial Chamber has to have in mind is that this is not the only trial. Not only is it not the only trial, there are another three cases on its docket, and some of the accused in those cases have been in custody for some time, and, therefore, we are going to have to consider how to arrange our work between the two cases. Now, this can only be, by way of preliminary thinking, allowed, it's no more than that, but I want to draw it to your attention because it will affect clearly the conduct of this case. So we need to know in order to plan our work, have some idea of the Defence position so that we can plan the work for the rest of the year. I don't know if you're in a position to deal with that. At least give us an indication, Mr. Stein, of what may be the progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me give you the bad news first and then the good, if I may. The resolution of this issue, of course, is dependent on how the Court resolves our motion to dismiss and to close the case. The issues of command and control and individual liability will be clearly addressed in that motion. The Court's ruling will shape what we need to do, obviously. Similarly, with regard to the Dr. Cigar issue and also the ex parte issues which we have dealt with and the time frame in which, if we are successful, we then can get evidence, use that evidence within the proper framework. So all those movable parts are about us. So that results, if everything goes awry, we believe, between a five to nine month trial for the Defence with 100 witnesses, if all things work adversely, and that's assuming full trial weeks. The good news, on the other hand, is Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Mikulicic and us met yesterday and we will continue to dialogue on whether or not much of what we do or some of what we do can be done jointly so there will be no overlap, and we're exploring that. So I would say at the outset, five to nine months because you need a number. I would not, however, if I may be so bold, suggest that that is something that should be etched in stone administrative-wise or otherwise because it is just too early. We'd love to do it in less; we hope not to do it in more. Five to nine months is a long window, and I appreciate that, and we will endeavour mightily to hone our case down so we can give you a specific time period for the Court's administrative purposes. The other aspect that drives the equation, frankly, is the time period between the Prosecution's case and our case, not set for argument, but it does drive our work. You may appreciate, I'm sure, that during the course of the trial, we have spent our time doing what we do, working on the matters at hand. The more time we have between the close of the Prosecution's case and the opening of our case to resolve the motion to dismiss, to resolve the evidence that will be coming in through co-operative States as well as non-co-operative States, and to generally get our house in order, the shorter our case will be. So those are the parameters in which I feel comfortable addressing the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, the same comments will be made about the Defence as we've been making on the Prosecution, on the need to cut down witnesses, to explore other methods of putting evidence before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I hope you will be exploring with the Prosecution, trying to agree matters, agree statements, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are whole areas which I would have thought are capable of agreement or non-dispute, matters, for instance, of character. I can remember in Kupreskic, for instance, that what we did -- of course, there were six accused, but what we did was allow, I think, one character witness per accused and then required affidavits for any remaining witnesses. That sort of thing and matters which go towards background of the offences, or certainly as far as the accused are concerned, all that, I would hope, is capable of swift resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. And I propose, having learned from one of my better colleagues on the other side about modern trial procedures and new innovative ideas, to perhaps be making some suggestions across the aisle as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you asked for a longer time; I indicated a shorter time earlier. That may have to be reviewed, what I said, in the light of our need to start other trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Along those lines, when we get to the issue of time between this case and the start of the Defence case, I think that is a window that the Court might look to in terms of its other work that could be consistent with our needs as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One suggestion is looking at the calendar, it's no more than a suggestion and can't be at this stage, if the Prosecution were to finish on the 10th of March, it's then a period of one week where we're not sitting and then another six weeks before the May sittings, post-Easter, Easter comes at the end of April, May the 1st, I recollect, is a holiday here, but May the 2nd would be a day when the Court would be sitting again after the Easter break, I anticipate. You might like to consider that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let us mull -- I'm sure Mr. Kovacic has his own views on these things, and when we next speak we'll be ready to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you must expect judicial involvement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- in how the case is presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It always boils down to are we given a straight May-through-June, eight weeks ours, this is our courtroom, or are we interspersed, as has been the case in the past, with other trials? Both of which -- neither of which is a perfect world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, I have endeavoured and will go on endeavouring to ensure that everybody is given the earliest possible indication of what the Trial Chamber proposes to do with its programme. There is at least a programme available, which I don't see why you shouldn't have, for May the 1st until September the 8th. We will be taking the month's recess. Of course, that's a matter which we've got to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would appreciate that programme. I'm sure the legal officer will give me one and we can work that into the mix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, since you are on your feet, and also Mr. Kovacic, when do you think you will be able to give us a list of your witnesses and possibly some idea about the substance of their testimonies, and when do you think you would be able to supply us with that list? I'm asking an identical question of Mr. Kovacic, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution, in this particular case, was ordered to supply us with that list on March 27th, as I recall, the trial starting on April 12th. I would think that certainly two weeks before the start of our trial we would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: That means in the middle of April or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Assuming we were to start on May the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: On May 1st. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the Rules about the pre-Defence conference which I will have to look at, and we'll see what the obligations are in that regard. Mr. Kovacic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a slight addition. As my colleague Stein said, we recognised earlier, and indeed yesterday we had, I guess, at least three meetings on the same topic, how to economise the Defence case, because certainly, as you understand, there are many issues on the level of general or preconditions or surroundings, et cetera, and that is the area where we can obviously save some time. Some of us are having a little bit different opinions on something so we are discussing how to put all that into one very compressed block. That is probably the best opportunity to economise the time, I guess. Otherwise, each Defence will go with its separate set of evidence and that won't be very rational, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean, there cannot be an overlap, we can't have witnesses saying the same things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So please work on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going even further, that is what I'm trying to say. It's not that we will have repetitive evidence on that part, but also that we can -- and we've already found some possibilities on that, that while discussing the matters amongst us, we are narrowing the issues as well. So instead of having, I don't know, three witnesses on one issue, we may do it with one or with two and then papers. So we do feel that it is a very important job, but there are many, many open issues still pending, and that, somehow, is harming us to speed up that process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there are any other matters which anyone wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only two, one entirely administrative. There is an organigramme, as I think I indicated, that's available for distribution in case it's of assistance. Momentarily for this hearing, if the Chamber would look at its list of ex parte applications relating to the Prosecution, number 11, that is the witness who was scheduled to attend today, or this week. Normally, we would deal with this by an ex parte hearing and suggest having an ex parte hearing in relation to it, but we can avoid that hearing if I simply tell you that the evidence or the material available in relation to that witness is exactly what is contained in the report of the security officer that we've already looked at in relation to other witnesses, it's no more and no less than that, and we would invite the Court, now that the witness has not attended, to read that material and, therefore, to deal with that witness in the same way as the Chamber will, in due course, deal with the other witnesses who've already shown themselves unwilling to respond to the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A report of the security officer? Remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Bromfield is his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The legal officer raises a point of a date when you want these witnesses to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that in order that the whole process can be gone through, including, as the Chamber knows, consideration of their evidence being read, if we could have them all timetabled to appear on the first week after the break, that would be the week of the 14th of February, then I think that should give us time for other steps to be taken if, as I rather fear, they may not be responsive. But if they are responsive, that week, we'll have to put other witnesses back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If the Prosecution can give us the 20 remaining witnesses in the order in which they're going to testify beyond the fortnight rule, it would be immensely helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I think they've got them all in earlier lists, but I'll give them our best/latest calculation via Ms. Bauer sometime today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then pass it on to the Trial Chamber too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Monday morning, please, at half past nine -- Tuesday. Tuesday morning at half past nine.
